title: Research projects
text:
In my research I have been interestesd in social science, epidemiological and environmental science topics. I have experience using advanced statistical methods and large-scale datasets to get data-driven insights that can inform public health, social policy, and clinical practice.
My academic journey began in psychological research, focusing on therapeutic interventions and clinical research. It then expanded into social policy and public health, and have recently finished my PhD where I specialized in using large registry data linkage to explore the interplay of environmental exposures and health outcomes at a population level.

title: Cross-country differences in the association between socioecnomic status and adolescent mental health
text: This project was my Master Thesis for the MSc. in Social Policy and Public Health at Utrecht University. We examined the association between adolescent socioeconomic status (SES), national-level mental health policies and adolescent mental health outcomes using data from 11-15 year-olds from 30 European Countries (n = 155.375).

title: Cross-country differences in the association between socioecnomic status and adolescent mental health
text: This project was my Master Thesis for the MSc. in Social Policy and Public Health at Utrecht University. We examined the association between adolescent socioeconomic status (SES), national-level mental health policies and adolescent mental health outcomes using data from 11-15 year-olds from 30 European Countries (n = 155.375).

title: Cross-country differences in the association between socioecnomic status and adolescent mental health
text:
Methodology

Multilevel regression analysis: Conducted using the lme4 and lmerTest package in R.

We used two-level linear regression models to investigate (1) overall associations between family affluence and adolescent mental health outcomes (2) overall associations between national-level policy indicators and adolescent mental health outcomes (3) cross country variations in the association between family affluence and adolescent mental health outcomes (4) the moderating role of national-level policy indicators on the association between family affluence and adolescent mental health outcomes.

title: Temporal Trends in Air Pollution Exposure across Socioeconomic Groups in The Netherlands
text: Air pollution exposure has been linked to detrimental health outcomes. While cross-sectional studies have demonstrated socioeconomic disparities in air pollution exposure, longitudinal evidence on these disparities remains limited. The current study investigates trends in residential air pollution exposure across socioeconomic groups in the Netherlands from 2014 to 2019.

title: Temporal Trends in Air Pollution Exposure across Socioeconomic Groups in The Netherlands
text: Air pollution exposure has been linked to detrimental health outcomes. While cross-sectional studies have demonstrated socioeconomic disparities in air pollution exposure, longitudinal evidence on these disparities remains limited. The current study investigates trends in residential air pollution exposure across socioeconomic groups in the Netherlands from 2014 to 2019.

title: Temporal Trends in Air Pollution Exposure across Socioeconomic Groups in The Netherlands
text:
Methodology
Our dataset includes over 12.5 million individuals, aged 18 years and above, who resided in the Netherlands between 2014 and 2019, using Statistics Netherlands data. The address-level air pollution concentrations were estimated by dispersion models of the National Institute of Public Health and the Environment. We linked the exposure estimations of particulate matter < 10 or <2.5 μm (PM10, PM2.5) and nitrogen dioxide (NO2) to household-level socioeconomic data.

title: A social identity approach to COVID-19 transmission in hospital settings
text: This project, funded by the Scottish Government, aimed to understand the barriers healthcare workers (HCWs) faced in adhering to COVID-19 safety guidelines. The research explored how psychological group processes influenced perceived risk of COVID-19 and adherence to safety measures in hospital settings.

title: A social identity approach to COVID-19 transmission in hospital settings

title: A social identity approach to COVID-19 transmission in hospital settings
text:
Methodology

Exploratory Factor Analysis: Conducted using the psych package in R to identify item clusters.
Mediation Analysis: Performed using the Lavaan package in R to explore relationships between variables.
Bootstrapped Sobel Test: Used to assess mediation effects with 10,000 samples for robustness.

title: Niklas Hlubek
text:
I’m Niklas, an interdisciplinary quantitative researcher interested in understanding complex societal challenges through data. My work integrates data from diverse sources, from survey and policy data to population registers and environmental datasets, to generate evidence-based insights.


In my current role as a PhD Research Fellow in Epidemiology at Utrecht University Medical Center, I study how social and environmental factors influence public health using nationwide longitudinal registry data. My research integrates causal inference, spatial analysis, and time-to-event modeling to generate evidence that can guide policy and improve urban well-being.


This work has been part of the European Union’s H2020 SURREAL Urban Health Network, a collaborative initiative focused on advancing research in sustainable and equitable urban health.

Core Competencies

Quantitative Analysis & Modeling – Longitudinal and spatial modeling for real-world data.

Evaluation & Monitoring – Designing studies and indicators to assess policy and intervention impact.

Data Visualization – Communicating insights through reports, presentations, and dashboards.

Interdisciplinary Collaboration – Bridging public health, psychology, environmental science, and policy.

title: Assessing the impact of changes in home location on adolescent lung function: An exposome-wide natural experiment
text: Residential relocation is common during childhood and influences multiple aspects of the living environment. This study contributes to a better understanding of how changes in complex environmental exposures interact to shape lung health. Our findings suggest that relocation to areas with higher levels of built-up surface environments - characterized by less green space and more impervious surfaces – is associated with reduced lung function in adolescents. These results highlight the need for further research in exposome and environmental epidemiology, expanding to more countries and additional health indicators to comprehensively assess the long-term health impacts of residential moves.

title: Assessing the impact of changes in home location on adolescent lung function: An exposome-wide natural experiment
text: Residential relocation is common during childhood and influences multiple aspects of the living environment. This study contributes to a better understanding of how changes in complex environmental exposures interact to shape lung health. Our findings suggest that relocation to areas with higher levels of built-up surface environments - characterized by less green space and more impervious surfaces – is associated with reduced lung function in adolescents. These results highlight the need for further research in exposome and environmental epidemiology, expanding to more countries and additional health indicators to comprehensively assess the long-term health impacts of residential moves.

title: Assessing the impact of changes in home location on adolescent lung function: An exposome-wide natural experiment
text:
Methodology
We characterized three external-exposome domains—air pollution, green/blue infrastructure, and area-level socioeconomic disadvantage—by rescaling cohort-specific exposures using interquartile ranges and applying a k-median clustering algorithm, which offers robustness to outliers and skewed distributions compared with k-means.
Exposome clusters were derived separately for each cohort, and relocation trajectories between ages 8 and 16 were defined based on relocation between low-, medium-, and high-hazard cluster levels. To estimate how changes in exposome clusters affected changes in lung-function, we used a difference-in-difference (DiD) framework with relocation trajectories as the exposure and incorporated inverse probability weighting (IPW) to reduce bias from selective relocation patterns. Weights were derived via the WeightIt package.

title: Assessing the impact of changes in home location on adolescent lung function: An exposome-wide natural experiment
